## Introduction and Rationale  

The introduction of real (and complex) numbers arises from the discovery that the rational number system ($\BB{Q}$) is inadequate in many scenarios. "Irrational numbers" is then introduced to fill the gap and is often approximated by rational numbers.  

Here's an example that shows the need of extension from the rational number system.  

::: {.callout-tip title="Example 1"}
We now show that    

$$\begin{aligned}
  p^2 &= 2
\end{aligned}$$

is not satisfied by **any** rational $p$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Example 1 Solution"}


Assume such $p$ exists. Since $p \in \BB{Q}$, we can denote this as $p = m/n$ where $m, n$ are integers that are not both even and $n \neq 0$.  

Rewrite the equation:  

$$\begin{aligned}
  m^2 &= 2 n^2
\end{aligned}$$

This shows that $m^2$ is even. $m$ is therefore even. It follows that both sides are divisible by $4$, hence $n^2$ and eventually $n$ is even.  

It all leads to a contradiction! Hence the equation is not satisfied by **any** $p \in \BB{Q}$. $\blacksquare$

___

One lovely extension of this proof is to show the following.  

Let $A$ be the set of $p \in \BB{Q}_+$ with $p^2 < 2$. Let $B$ be the set of $p \in \BB{Q}_+$ with $p^2 > 2$. Show that there exists a $q \in \BB{Q}_+$ such that:  

- $p < q$ for every $p \in A$
- $p > q$ for every $p \in B$

**Solution.** We just simply associate every $p > 0$ with:  

$$\begin{aligned}
  q &= p - \frac{p^2 - 2}{p + 2}
\end{aligned}$$


:::
